video_title: Don Wilson on the GPU Market's Trillion Dollar Question | Odd Lots
gist: Don Wilson of DRW explains why GPU futures (CME listing possible Nov 9) are needed to hedge compute price and residual-value risk and cut neocloud financing costs, floats token futures and a 'crunch spread', and defends perpetual futures.

insights.claim: Wilson reads the recent AI-trade jitters (CoreWeave, a reported Anthropic pre-IPO investor meeting with slightly slower revenue growth) as expected volatility, not a slowdown, because growth this fast cannot have constant first or second derivatives.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Short-term growth wobbles in AI revenue are not evidence of a trend break.
insights.quote: that first derivatives isn't going to be constant. The second derivative isn't going to be constant.

themes.theme: GPU futures and neocloud cost of capital

insights.claim: A CoreWeave debt yield around 15% shows the need for risk-management products: neoclouds selling on-demand compute or to less creditworthy customers face higher cost of capital than those with contracts from the most creditworthy firms.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Unhedged revenue streams are priced punitively in credit markets, creating demand for a hedge.

insights.claim: With GPU futures, a neocloud could buy GPUs, sell a strip of futures, and then sell on-demand compute or six-month contracts to weaker credits (who post a large share upfront); Wilson expects the market to reward this with much lower cost of capital.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Futures could compress financing costs for GPU-backed lenders and borrowers.

insights.claim: CFTC comment period on compute futures was extended; absent action, futures can list November 9, conveniently after November 3. Wilson cannot explain the regulatory concern; one theory he has heard is that some indices are not robust.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Listing date of Nov 9 is a near-term catalyst for the compute-derivatives market.

insights.claim: Wilson says index robustness is a buyer-beware matter; Silicon Data collects extensive on-demand cloud data and is building an IOSCO-compliant index, whereas hyperscalers are few and neoclouds many with transparent on-demand pricing, despite many GPUs being sold via opaque bilateral offtake deals.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Index quality is the main attack surface for compute futures and will differentiate providers.

insights.claim: Initial CME GPU futures will go out three years and extend as liquidity grows, letting holders hedge the unknown future value of chips like an A100 or H100, which Wilson calls the trillion-dollar question.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Residual-value risk is the core thing GPU lenders cannot currently hedge.

insights.claim: H100 hourly on-demand prices fell through most of 2025, then turned up around Thanksgiving when Anthropic's newest model drove a surge in inference demand; more recently B200, B300 and H100 prices surged again while the Silicon Data token index plummeted.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: GPU rental prices and token prices can diverge, so hardware and token exposure are separate risks.

insights.claim: Wilson rejects the worry that hedging lets people overbuild: a futures sale needs a rational buyer, so forward prices will sit lower given heavy producer hedging demand, with investors buying futures for return.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Hedging supply will push the forward curve down, which should discipline leverage rather than enable it.

insights.claim: Demand for a futures market already exists beyond bilateral deals between Anthropic/OpenAI and hyperscalers because open-source model hosting has exploded, with multi-billion-dollar firms like Fireworks and Together selling tokens on rented GPUs.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: A fragmented inference ecosystem is what makes a liquid compute market viable.

insights.claim: On heterogeneity objections (AMD, Cerebras, Trainium, TPUs, software stacks), Wilson argues H100 or B200 alone has enough money to support a single contract, related chips are highly correlated so tradable as basis, and training-cluster premiums track inference demand.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Contracts will target standard baseline configurations, with other hardware priced via basis.

insights.claim: Each new chip generation needs its own contract and liquidity pool, but DRW would only list the major ones, like electricity and oil which have many contracts.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Liquidity fragmentation across generations is a manageable cost.

themes.theme: Token futures and the crunch spread

insights.claim: Wilson expects futures on tokens themselves eventually; renting GPUs at the on-demand price and selling open-source-model tokens via a router would earn a margin analogous to an oil crack spread or soybean crush spread, which he jokingly calls the crunch spread.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: A token/GPU spread would let inference providers hedge margins; Wilson says it is at the thought stage.
insights.quote: We call this the crunch spread.

themes.theme: Nvidia and AI adoption at DRW

insights.claim: Wilson thinks Nvidia is unlikely to maintain its current market share but is confident Nvidia will keep growing because the overall space will keep growing.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Share loss to rivals is compatible with continued Nvidia growth.

insights.claim: DRW's AI use has moved to more front-line adoption over the year and token use is rising exponentially; its main optimisation is routing inference requests so not every request goes to a frontier model, minimising token spend.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Model routing is the lever firms use to control exploding token budgets.

insights.claim: Wilson argues perps are futures contracts with a useful economic purpose: a crude oil ETF holding a Brent perp would avoid the roll slippage of today's ETFs that hold the first few futures contracts.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Perps could cut roll costs for commodity ETFs while monthly and quarterly futures still serve producers hedging far out the curve.

insights.claim: A retail holder of a hard-to-borrow stock gets none of the borrow fee hedge funds pay (he cites 100% annualised), whereas holding a perp would mechanically pass that funding through.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Perps could let retail capture economic value that brokers currently keep.

insights.claim: Leverage and auto-deleveraging are not inherent to perps: a quarterly future can have them, and a perp could be listed with reasonable leverage and no auto-deleveraging; Wilson says the future-versus-swap distinction is mere nomenclature, since a cleared swap carries the same risk as a future.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Regulatory objections to perps based on expiry or leverage are weak on economic grounds.

insights.claim: Wilson says 24/7 trading is inevitable and already here; DRW has traded crypto since 2014, but its options market makers are unhappy about making SOFR options markets over weekends.
insights.speaker: Don Wilson
insights.so_what: Round-the-clock markets will pressure market-maker economics in rate options.
